title: Graph Representation
why: Every graph algorithm starts here. Adjacency lists are the CP default: O(V+E) memory and O(deg) neighbour iteration. Getting the input-reading boilerplate automatic means graph problems start at the algorithm, not at plumbing.
traps: Input is almost always 1-indexed. Either size your arrays n+1 or subtract 1 at read time — and be consistent.
Forgetting to add the reverse edge for undirected graphs. Half your BFS silently doesn't traverse.
Using an adjacency *matrix* for n = 10^5 — that's 10^10 cells. Matrices are only for n <= ~2000.
Assuming the graph is connected. Many problems hand you a forest, and you must loop over all start vertices.

template.py:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, m = map(int, input().split())
adj = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]           # 1-indexed
for _ in range(m):
    u, v = map(int, input().split())
    adj[u].append(v)
    adj[v].append(u)                        # omit for directed

wadj = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
wadj[u].append((v, w))

pyNote: Build with `[[] for _ in range(n+1)]` — never `[[]]*(n+1)`, which aliases one list n+1 times and is the most destructive Python graph bug there is.
checkpoint: You can read a weighted undirected graph and iterate neighbours from memory, 1-indexed, in both languages.

title: Breadth-First Search
why: BFS gives shortest paths on **unweighted** graphs — the first time you reach a vertex is via a minimum-edge-count path. Multi-source BFS (seed the queue with every source at distance 0) answers 'distance to the nearest X' for the whole grid in one pass.
traps: Marking visited when *popping* instead of when *pushing*. That lets a vertex enter the queue many times and degrades to O(V*E).
Using BFS on a weighted graph. It's only correct when all edge weights are equal (use Dijkstra or 0-1 BFS otherwise).
Forgetting to initialise distances to -1 / infinity so you can distinguish 'unreachable' from 'distance 0'.
In grids, not converting (r, c) to a single index — or doing it inconsistently.

template.py:
from collections import deque

dist = [-1] * (n + 1)
q = deque([src])
dist[src] = 0

while q:
    u = q.popleft()
    for v in adj[u]:
        if dist[v] != -1: continue
        dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
        q.append(v)

# multi-source
q = deque(sources)
for s in sources: dist[s] = 0

pyNote: `collections.deque` is mandatory — `list.pop(0)` is O(n) and turns your BFS into O(V^2). BFS is also the safe way to traverse big graphs in Python, since it avoids the recursion limit entirely.
checkpoint: You can solve a multi-source grid BFS (e.g. distance to the nearest exit) in one pass.

title: DFS & Connected Components
why: DFS explores depth-first, which makes it the natural fit for component labelling, cycle detection, and anything needing entry/exit times. Most tree algorithms are DFS with extra bookkeeping.
traps: **Python recursion depth.** A path graph with 10^5 nodes recurses 10^5 deep and crashes. Write DFS iteratively in Python for anything beyond small inputs.
Cycle detection differs by graph type: undirected needs a 'skip the parent' check; directed needs three colours (white/grey/black), because seeing a visited node isn't enough.
Not resetting state between test cases, so component IDs leak across cases.
In C++, deep recursion can blow the 256 MB stack too — it's rarer, but real at 10^6 depth.
pyNote: The `(node, is_post_order)` stack trick is the standard way to get post-order work — subtree sizes, tree DP — out of an iterative DFS. Learn this pattern now; you will reuse it for every tree problem.
checkpoint: You can write an iterative DFS with post-order processing, and detect cycles in both directed and undirected graphs.

title: Dynamic Programming: Foundations
why: DP is brute force plus memoisation: define a state that captures everything you need about the past, write the transition, and each state is computed once. The whole skill is choosing the state — the transition usually writes itself.
traps: A state that doesn't capture enough information, so the same state gives different answers depending on how you got there. If that happens, your state is incomplete.
Wrong iteration order in bottom-up: every dependency must be computed before it's used.
Not initialising the base case, or using 0 as 'unset' when 0 is a legitimate answer. Use -1 or -infinity.
Recursive memoisation in Python hitting the recursion limit — convert to bottom-up for large states.
pyNote: `@lru_cache` (or `@cache` in 3.9+) turns any pure recursive function into a memoised one for free — unbeatable for prototyping. But it is slow and recursion-limited, so convert hot DP to bottom-up loops before submitting.
checkpoint: You can state any DP's state definition as one English sentence before writing code.

title: Knapsack & Subset DP
why: The canonical 'choose a subset under a constraint' family. 0/1 knapsack, unbounded knapsack, subset-sum, and coin change are one idea with four transition shapes — and the space-optimised 1D rolling array is a template you'll reuse for years.
traps: The loop direction in the 1D version is the whole trick: **descending** weight for 0/1 (each item once), **ascending** for unbounded (items reusable). Get it backwards and you silently solve the other problem.
Counting vs optimising: counting the number of ways needs `dp[w] += dp[w - wt]`, not `max`.
Capacity too large for a DP table. If W is 10^9, knapsack is the wrong tool — look for meet-in-the-middle or a greedy structure.
Forgetting that the 2D version needs the previous row, so you can't overwrite in place without the direction trick.

template.py:
# 0/1 knapsack
dp = [0] * (W + 1)
for i in range(n):
    for w in range(W, wt[i] - 1, -1):              # DESCENDING
        dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i])

# unbounded
for i in range(n):
    for w in range(wt[i], W + 1):                  # ASCENDING
        dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i])

# subset-sum with a big int as a bitset - C-speed, enormously faster
can = 1
for x in a:
    can |= can << x
reachable = (can >> target) & 1

pyNote: The big-int bitset trick is Python's secret weapon for subset-sum: `can |= can << x` shifts an arbitrary-precision integer at C speed, matching C++'s `bitset` without any of the size-must-be-constant restrictions. This single idiom rescues many otherwise-TLE knapsack problems.
checkpoint: You can explain why 0/1 knapsack iterates weight descending, and derive it rather than memorise it.

title: Counting & Binomials
why: Factorials and inverse factorials precomputed once give nCr mod p in O(1) per query. Beyond that, the core skill is modelling: recognising a count as arrangements, combinations, or stars-and-bars.
traps: Recomputing an inverse per query. Precompute the whole inverse-factorial array in O(n) using the backwards recurrence.
nCr with r < 0 or r > n must return 0, not crash or wrap around.
Confusing permutations (order matters) with combinations (it doesn't). Write down a tiny case and count by hand to check.
Overflow before the modulus is applied — reduce at every multiplication.

template.py:
MOD = 10**9 + 7
N = 2 * 10**5 + 5

fact = [1] * N
for i in range(1, N): fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD
invf = [1] * N
invf[N-1] = pow(fact[N-1], MOD - 2, MOD)
for i in range(N-1, 0, -1): invf[i-1] = invf[i] * i % MOD

def C(n, r):
    if r < 0 or r > n: return 0
    return fact[n] * invf[r] % MOD * invf[n-r] % MOD

# exact small values without a modulus:
from math import comb, perm, factorial
comb(10, 3)     # 120, arbitrary precision

pyNote: `math.comb(n, r)` gives exact binomials with no modulus and no overflow — perfect when the problem doesn't ask for a modulus, or for checking your modular implementation against ground truth.
checkpoint: You can answer 10^5 nCr-mod-p queries in O(n + q) total.

title: Greedy with Exchange Arguments
why: The step from 'greedy that happens to work' to 'greedy I can prove'. An exchange argument shows that any optimal solution can be transformed into the greedy one without getting worse — which both proves correctness and, run backwards, *tells you the sort order*.
traps: Skipping the proof on hard problems. At 1600+, the plausible-looking greedy is frequently wrong.
Not considering the tiebreak, which the exchange argument often pins down exactly.
Greedy on a problem with a global constraint coupling choices — that's DP or flow territory.
Forgetting to stress test. Even a proof you believe deserves 1000 random small cases.

template.py:
from functools import cmp_to_key

# ratio comparator without floating point
def cmp(x, y):
    return (x[0] * y[1] > y[0] * x[1]) - (x[0] * y[1] < y[0] * x[1])

v.sort(key=cmp_to_key(cmp))

# prefer a plain key when you can derive one - much faster than cmp_to_key
v.sort(key=lambda p: p[0] / p[1])       # only if precision is safe

pyNote: `cmp_to_key` works but is slow (a Python call per comparison). Derive a tuple or fraction key when possible; `Fraction` from the stdlib gives exact ratio keys without floating-point risk.
checkpoint: You can derive the correct sort comparator from an adjacent-swap argument rather than guessing it.

title: Heaps & Priority Queues
why: When a greedy needs 'the best remaining option' and the set changes as you go, a heap gives it in O(log n). This powers scheduling problems, Dijkstra, k-way merges, and the 'keep the k best so far' pattern.
traps: C++ `priority_queue` is a **max**-heap; Python's `heapq` is a **min**-heap. Both defaults surprise people. Negate values to flip.
No decrease-key operation. The standard workaround is to push duplicates and skip stale entries on pop.
Heapifying an existing list is O(n) with `heapify` / the range constructor, but O(n log n) if you push one at a time.
Comparing tuples in Python where the second element isn't comparable — if two priorities tie, Python compares the next field and can raise TypeError.

template.py:
import heapq

h = []
heapq.heappush(h, x)
smallest = heapq.heappop(h)
heapq.heapify(a)                   # O(n), in place

# max-heap: negate on the way in and out
heapq.heappush(h, -x)
largest = -heapq.heappop(h)

# k largest in O(n log k)
h = []
for x in a:
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
    if len(h) > k: heapq.heappop(h)

# tuples: put a tiebreak field in so comparison never reaches a non-comparable
heapq.heappush(pq, (dist, node))
top_k = heapq.nlargest(k, a)       # convenience, C-speed

pyNote: `heapq` operates on a plain list, so `heapq.heapify(a)` is O(n) in place. `nlargest`/`nsmallest` handle the common case in one call. Remember it is min-only — negate for max.
checkpoint: You can maintain a running median or the k largest elements of a stream using heaps.

title: Interval Problems
why: Merging, counting overlaps, and scheduling all reduce to sorting by the right endpoint and sweeping. The sweep-line view — turn each interval into a +1 event at the start and a -1 at the end, then sort events — generalises to almost everything.
traps: Whether endpoints are inclusive or exclusive changes whether touching intervals merge. Read carefully.
Event ordering at equal coordinates: process starts before ends (or the reverse) depending on whether touching counts as overlap.
Sorting by start when the problem wants end (activity selection) or vice versa.
Coordinates up to 10^9 make a difference array impossible — compress first, or use events.

template.py:
iv.sort()
merged = []
for s, e in iv:
    if merged and s <= merged[-1][1]:
        merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], e)
    else:
        merged.append([s, e])

# sweep line
ev = []
for s, e in iv:
    ev.append((s, 1))
    ev.append((e, -1))
ev.sort()
cur = best = 0
for x, d in ev:
    cur += d
    best = max(best, cur)

checkpoint: You can compute maximum simultaneous overlap with a sweep line and justify your event tiebreak.

title: Coordinate Compression
why: Values up to 10^9 but only 10^5 of them? Map them to 0..k-1 preserving order. This is the bridge that lets you use array-indexed structures (Fenwick trees, difference arrays, DP tables) on huge value ranges.
traps: Compressing values but then comparing against uncompressed ones later in the code.
Forgetting to include query coordinates in the compression, not just the input values.
Losing the ability to output original values — keep the sorted unique array to map back.
Using `lower_bound` on an unsorted array. The compression array must be sorted and deduplicated first.

template.py:
import bisect

vals = sorted(set(a + [l for l, r in queries] + [r for l, r in queries]))
idx = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(vals)}     # dict lookup: O(1)

a = [idx[x] for x in a]
original = vals[compressed]

# or with bisect when you can't build the dict
i = bisect.bisect_left(vals, x)

pyNote: A dict built from `enumerate(vals)` gives O(1) compression lookups versus `bisect`'s O(log n), and reads more clearly. Build the dict when you'll do many lookups.
checkpoint: You can compress 10^5 coordinates from a 10^9 range and map answers back to originals.
